column4: The source defines a dāll as one who is جائر عن القصد; this ayah sets قَصْدُ ٱلسَّبِيلِ against roads that are جَائِرٌ and makes guidance God's act, giving that dictionary line a Qur'anic road.
After God has guided them, people are asked whether they should turn back on their heels; the same ayah stages a bewildered man in the land whose companions stand ahead calling him toward guidance.
A traveler in darkness sees a distant fire and hopes either for a brand or to find guidance there, joining finding and guidance at the exact point where the night road fails.
Moses sets out toward Midian and asks his Lord to guide him to سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, the middle or right line of the road invoked by the source's definition of deviation.
The stars are furnished so travelers may find their way through the darknesses of land and sea; this is the section's invisible night road supplied with guides.
The question “Who guides you in the darknesses of land and sea?” makes divine guidance the answer to the traveler's concrete inability to see a route.
Moses names a destination, the meeting of the two seas, and refuses to cease until he reaches it; this embodies continuing on one's course toward the intended place.
At the very junction Moses seeks, the travelers overlook the fish and lose the sign of arrival; the destination is reached before it is recognized.
The servant recalls that when they took refuge at the rock, أَوَيْنَا, the fish escaped along its way; shelter, a missed sign, and a path meet in one travel scene.
Moses recognizes the sought marker and the pair return, retracing their own footprints; backward movement here repairs rather than abandons the route.
After recovering the place, they find a divinely taught servant; وَجَدَا marks the moment the lost destination yields the guide Moses was seeking.
Moses asks to follow the servant so that he may teach him right guidance, a literal follower placing himself behind a guide who goes ahead.
Moses is commanded to lead the servants by night and make a dry road through the sea, with neither fear of being overtaken nor of losing the way.
God commands Moses to depart with the servants by night because they will be pursued, establishing the dangerous dark journey whose way God then opens.
When the two hosts see one another, Moses' companions believe they have been caught; the apparent end of the road creates the need answered in 26:62-63.
At the blocked sea Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him, locating guidance at the instant no route can yet be seen.
The sea is split after Moses strikes it, so an impossible boundary becomes the route promised by his words in 26:62.
Moses tells his family that he perceives a fire and may return with news or a burning brand; this repeated scene supplies the family traveler and the distant night marker behind 20:10.
Traveling with his family after completing his term, Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring news from it; the ayah makes explicit that the fire appears during a journey whose direction is uncertain.
The believers' light runs before them as they approach the gardens, a visible realization of the guide who advances ahead of the traveler toward the final dwelling.
God promises believers a light by which they walk, turning guidance in darkness into a carried means of travel.
One given light walks among people, unlike one trapped in darkness and unable to emerge; the contrast makes visible what it means for a road to appear after concealment.
By revelation God guides seekers into paths of peace, brings them from darkness into light, and guides them to a straight path; all three movements of the section converge here.
The Book is sent to bring people from darkness into light and onto the path of the Mighty, making revelation the forward guide through an unseen road.
Moses is told to bring his people from darkness into light; the prophet who was guided on his own journeys now becomes the guide of a people.
A thirsty traveler reaches what he took for water and finds it nothing, but finds God there; وَجَدَهُ and وَوَجَدَ ٱللَّهَ reverse the expected destination and the act of finding.
Layered darkness at sea leaves a person scarcely able to see even his hand, and without God-given light there is no light; this is the section's inability to pick out a road intensified.
If sight were effaced, people would race toward the path but could not see it; the ayah directly separates having a road from being able to discern it.
If fixed or transformed in place, people could neither proceed nor return, setting forward travel and backward movement at the boundary of bodily ability.
The ayah asks whether one who walks fallen on his face is better guided than one walking upright on a straight path, giving guidance a bodily posture and traversable line.
Visible towns and measured stages let travelers journey safely by nights and days; the route remains legible even at the time the section's traveler cannot endure.
The servant is carried by night from the Sacred Mosque to the farther mosque and shown signs; this is a complete dark journey between named sacred destinations under divine conduct.
Lot is told to leave with his family during part of the night and that none should turn back; safe passage depends on obeying the given direction without looking behind.
Lot is commanded to travel with his family at night, keep behind them, forbid backward looks, and go exactly where commanded, joining guide position, route, and perseverance.
God invites to the House of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining the route, its guide, and the home in which the journey ends.
The first House established for humankind is blessed and a guidance for the worlds; the destination-house itself functions as guidance.
Pilgrimage is owed by whoever is able to find a way to the House, making السَّبِيلِ إِلَيْهِ the concrete route toward the home named in 3:96.
The House is made a place of return and security, so arrival is both repeated homecoming and refuge, the two senses attached to أَوَى in the section.
God assigns Abraham the site of the House and commands its preparation for those who come to it, a divinely disclosed destination before the travelers are summoned.
The pilgrimage call brings people on foot and lean mounts from every distant pass, filling the road to the House identified in 22:26.
The emigrant leaves home on God's road and will find many places of escape and abundance in the earth; the ayah joins departure, finding, shelter, provision, and even a journey cut short by death.
God reminds an endangered, uprooted community that He sheltered them, supported them, and provided good things; آوَاكُمْ repeats the sheltering gift of 93:6 and sets it beside provision.
Emigrants who leave home are paired with those who shelter and help them, so the journey ends through human hosts enacting the divine shelter named in the source.
The youths take refuge in the cave, أَوَى, and ask their Lord to prepare right guidance for their affair; shelter and guidance are sought together.
The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease; the destination becomes a shelter fitted for them.
The moving sun marks the sheltered cave, then the ayah says the one God guides is guided and the one He leaves astray will find no protecting guide; daylight, refuge, finding, and guidance converge.

When opponents fear that following guidance will uproot them, the reply points to a secure sanctuary to which fruits are brought as provision; guidance, safe home, and enrichment answer their fear together.
Abraham settles his family by the Sacred House in a barren valley and asks that hearts incline toward them and fruits provide for them, binding destination, dwelling, and provision.
A visitation reaches the garden by night while its owners sleep, so the change in their destination occurs while darkness hides it.
By morning the garden has become like a stripped or darkened field; dawn reveals that the travelers' intended place is no longer what they expected.
At daybreak the owners call one another to set out, supplying the morning departure that leads to their mistaken declaration of being lost.
They urge one another to go early to their crop, naming the destination and purpose of the dawn journey.
On seeing the altered garden they say إِنَّا لَضَآلُّونَ, first construing the lost destination as having taken the wrong way.
They correct themselves: they are not merely lost but deprived, مَحْرُومُونَ; the correction meets the section's link between directional loss and need.
The night sign is erased and the day sign made sight-giving so people may seek bounty; daylight provides the visibility and provision associated with the source's daytime traveler.
God darkens the night and brings out its morning brightness, ضُحَىٰهَا; the same named root marks the transition by which a hidden road can appear.
The night is sworn by as it covers, supplying the concealing half of the road image that 92:2 reverses.
The day is sworn by as it becomes manifest, directly reversing the night's covering and echoing the source gloss in which the road “becomes apparent.”
Within the same night-and-day surah, God declares that guidance belongs to Him, placing the giver of direction behind the alternation of concealment and disclosure.
God makes the sun a guide for the extending shadow; the ayah calls the source of daylight a دَلِيل, the very term the section explains as one who goes ahead.
The lamp inside layered glass culminates in “light upon light,” and God guides to His light; it supplies a luminous guide rather than leaving the traveler in darkness.
God brings believers out of darknesses into light while false patrons move people the other way, rendering guidance as opposed directions across the night-light boundary.
Clear signs are sent down to bring people from darkness into light, repeating the movement from a concealed world into one in which a way can be seen.
The worshiper directly asks, ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ, placing the traveler behind the guide and naming the road sought.
The road is identified as that of recipients of favor and distinguished from the way of those who are lost, joining gift, route, and ضَالِّينَ in one destination.
At humanity's descent to earth, those who follow God's guidance are promised freedom from fear and grief, paralleling the same Adamic road promise in 20:123.
Whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has ضَلَّ سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, losing precisely the middle of the way that Moses asks to be shown in 28:22.
The qiblah distinguishes one who follows the Messenger from one who turns on his heels, while the change is hard except for those God guided; direction, guide, and backward reversal meet.
Pilgrims are told to remember God as He guided them, though before that they were among the lost; remembrance becomes the response to having been shown the road.
Those already guided pray that their hearts not deviate afterward; guidance here requires remaining in the received course rather than turning aside.
Holding fast to God is described as having been guided to a straight path, giving the source's instruction to stay in one's course a Qur'anic formulation.
God identifies one straight path, commands that it be followed, and forbids the many paths that would split travelers away from it.
Those who follow the Messenger also follow the light sent with him; guide, follower, and traveling light form one relation.
The Prophet is commanded to call all people to faith and they are told to follow him so that they may be guided, making the guided messenger a guide for followers.
Abraham tells his father to follow him and promises to guide him onto a level path, the clearest interpersonal staging of the guide walking before another.
After descent to earth, whoever follows God's guidance will neither lose the way nor fall into misery, making faithful following the direct opposite of the source's lost traveler.
Prophets are made leaders who guide by God's command, embodying the section's explanation that the guide precedes those being led.
Those who strive toward God are promised guidance in His ways, so sustained movement is answered by routes rather than a single momentary indication.
Leaders are appointed to guide by God's command when they remain patient and certain, joining guidance from ahead with perseverance in the course.
People are told to follow messengers who ask no payment and are themselves guided; the one ahead is fit to guide because he has first received guidance.
Worship of God is named “a straight path” between the prohibition on following Satan and the reminder that Satan led many astray.
Abraham announces that he is going to his Lord and that his Lord will guide him, stating movement, destination, and guide in one first-person journey.
The believing man tells his people to follow him and promises to guide them to the way of right direction, standing before them against Pharaoh's rival claim.
The Prophet once did not know Book or faith, but the revealed light now lets him guide to a straight path; the guided one has become the guide.
The Prophet is told to hold fast to what was revealed because he is on a straight path, matching the source's instruction to keep to one's current word or work without veering.
The jinn describe the Book after Moses as guiding to truth and to a straight road; transmitted speech takes the guide's place before hearers who can follow.
God promises to guide the same prophetic addressee to a straight path, a direct counterpart to the remembered favor in 93:7.
The heard recitation guides to right conduct, so the revealed word itself becomes the guide encountered by its listeners.
God says He showed the human being the way, leaving gratitude or ingratitude as the response after direction has been supplied.
The question “Where, then, are you going?” exposes uncertainty about direction before 81:28 names the possibility of taking a straight course.
The reminder is for whoever wills to go straight, giving the bewildered addressee of 81:26 a course to choose and remain upon.
God says He guided the human being to the two ascending ways, presenting guidance as disclosure of divergent roads that demand a choice.
Moses names his former condition with ضَالِّينَ; as the section observes, the later speaker and guide first recalls himself as one without the right direction.
Moses says that after he fled, his Lord granted him judgment and made him a messenger; gift and commissioning answer the former lost state in 26:20.
God makes the earth a resting place and places roads in it so people may be guided, joining habitable ground with traversable direction.
The earth is made a cradle and roads are threaded through it, furnishing the physical field on which the section's traveler can move.
Broad passes are placed through the earth's mountains so people may be guided, making the created road itself an act of guidance.
Mountains, rivers, and roads are placed on earth so people may find their way; 16:16 then supplies landmarks and stars for the same journey.
Landmarks and stars are means by which people are guided, continuing the physical road scene of 16:15 into night.
Pharaoh goes before his people on Judgment Day and brings them to the Fire; the section's defining sign of a guide, preceding followers, is retained while the destination is reversed.
Pharaoh leads his people astray and does not guide them, naming the failed leader immediately after Moses has opened their night road.
The command “guide them to the path of Hell” preserves guide, path, and destination but makes every element carry the opposite end.
Pharaoh claims that he guides his people only to the way of right conduct; 40:38 exposes the rival claim by offering a guide whose destination is salvation.
Leaders are made who call toward the Fire, a direct reversal of leaders who walk ahead toward a safe home.
The condemned say they obeyed their leaders and great ones, who led them away from the road; following someone ahead does not by itself make that person a true guide.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray and guided to the punishment of the Blaze, a false guide carrying a follower to the wrong destination.
The ayah asks whether one who guides to truth deserves following more than one unable to guide unless first guided, defining the fitness of the one placed ahead.
The Prophet cannot guide everyone he loves, while God guides whom He wills; this sets a boundary around the guided Prophet's guiding role described in 42:52.
The Prophet's companion is declared neither to have strayed nor erred; this protects his revelatory stance while 93:7 can still recall a prior need for divine direction.
The Prophet says that any straying would fall on himself, whereas his guidance comes through revelation, explicitly locating the source of the guide's own direction.
Satan first presents himself as a protecting companion, then turns back on his heels and disowns his followers; the apparent guide abandons them by the source's backward motion.
Moses commands his people to enter the holy land and not turn on their backs or become losers, tying backward retreat to refusal of a named destination.
The holy land is barred and the people wander through the earth for forty years, the direct condition of travelers denied arrival and unable to complete their route.
Noah's son says he will take refuge on a mountain, but the chosen shelter cannot save him; أَوَى is exposed as a false arrival-place.
Hypocrites ask to borrow the believers' forward-running light and are told to turn back to seek light, after which a barrier divides the two groups.
Barriers are set before and behind people and their sight is covered, so neither the road ahead nor retreat can be seen.
One blind here will be blinder in the Hereafter and farther astray from the way, joining failed sight to loss of route.
The Prophet cannot guide the blind out of their wandering; bodily inability to see becomes the boundary image for accepting direction.
Thamud prefer blindness to guidance, choosing precisely the perceptual state in which the section's road disappears.
Devilish companions bar people from the path while those people suppose themselves guided, showing that confidence in direction can coexist with actual loss.
People turn back after guidance has become clear, so the section's rearward movement becomes deliberate abandonment of a disclosed route.
After Moses' people deviate, God causes their hearts to deviate; the ayah makes turning from the received line the opposite of staying in one's guidance.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are worst in place and most astray from the road, reversing upright guided walking and a safe destination.
The people ask for greater distances between their stages and are scattered, undoing the visible, measured, safe night-and-day route described in 34:18.
Their striving is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well, so a person can miss the intended line of action without recognizing the deviation.
The ayah denies that blindness and sight or darknesses and light are equal, articulating the perceptual boundary presupposed by the hidden and revealed road.
The blind and the seeing are not equal, introducing the capacity boundary that the darkness-light opposition in 35:20 completes.
Darknesses and light are not equal, the elemental reversal behind whether the traveler can discern a way.
At judgment the objects people fabricated vanish from them; what they depended on as a destination or support is itself the thing no longer to be found.
When the promised outcome arrives, fabricated objects of worship vanish from their devotees, reversing the traveler's expectation that the sought object will be waiting.
Every soul meets what it sent ahead and the invented gods vanish, so arrival discloses that the presumed destination was absent.
Those who lose themselves find their fabrications gone from them; the ayah couples self-loss with loss of the relied-on object.
On the day of submission, what people fabricated vanishes from them, making the thing formerly pursued unavailable at arrival.
After each community is called for proof, fabricated gods vanish; the failed object of reliance cannot guide or be found when demanded.
People confess that those they invoked have vanished from them, an after-arrival recognition that the sought supports were never a true destination.
Former objects of prayer vanish and their worshipers know there is no escape, pairing a lost false destination with the absence of a route away.
The supposed gods fail to help and vanish because they were fabricated, showing false guides and destinations disappearing at the point of need.
The Prophet says he would find neither protector nor refuge apart from God; the negative وَأَجِدَ ... مُلْتَحَدًا marks the boundary beyond which no shelter can be reached.
A second summary names the believers who migrated and those who sheltered and helped them, confirming that آوَوْا is an enacted response to displacement.
During the migration the Prophet and his companion occupy a cave while God grants tranquility and unseen support; it is a journey interrupted by divinely secured refuge.
A caravan seeking water finds a boy at the well, so a lost young person is literally found by travelers; the parallel is specific though Joseph's later lodging is supplied in 12:21.
The Egyptian who takes Joseph home tells his wife to make his stay honorable, completing the movement from being found on the road to being lodged in a house.
At the end of the brothers' journey Joseph receives his brother to himself, using آوَى for protective family arrival.
Joseph receives his parents to himself and tells the family to enter Egypt safely, presenting family reunion as the secure end of a long route.
Mary and her son are sheltered, آوَيْنَاهُمَا, on elevated settled ground with flowing water; refuge is made physically habitable and provisioned.
After asking for guidance to the middle of the road, Moses reaches Midian's water; this ayah supplies the first recognized arrival following 28:22.
A woman comes to Moses, leads him to her father, and the father declares him safe; the guided journey to Midian ends in an offered household and security.
Moses is again commanded to take God's servants away by night because they will be pursued, a repeated dark-road scene whose opened path is explicit elsewhere.
A light and clear Book are said to have come from God; 5:16 states how that light guides seekers through darkness and along paths of peace.
The Prophet's searching gaze is answered with a commanded direction toward the Sacred Mosque, concretizing the source's example of being unable to find the mosque.
Every community has a direction toward which it turns; the ayah addresses orientation rather than a traveled road, but directly meets the source's secondary image of not knowing which way to seek.
After a covenant of worship and support, whoever disbelieves is said to have lost سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, another use of deviation from the road's middle.
God does not let a people stray after guiding them until He clarifies what they must avoid, making continued guidance depend on a disclosed boundary.
Every people is said to have a guide; this supports the section's personal guide image, though the ayah does not stage the road itself.
The messengers ask why they should not rely on God when He has guided them in their ways, using plural routes for lives that must be patiently continued.
After the instruction to remember God when one forgets, the speaker asks to be guided to something nearer to right conduct; recovered memory becomes renewed direction.
Night is made a covering and day a rising into activity; beside the sun-guide of 25:45, this explains the daily change in the traveler's field of sight.
The addressee is told to follow the way of one who turns to God and is then reminded of the final return, joining a human route to its destination.
The disputants ask David to guide them to the even road, سَوَآءِ ٱلصِّرَاطِ; judicial direction is expressed through the same middle-of-the-way image.
One whose breast God opens is upon a light from his Lord; the ayah locates a guided person in illumination even though it does not describe literal travel.
The Prophet is commanded to call, remain straight as ordered, and not follow desires; this closely matches the source gloss “continue in your speech or work and do not turn from it.”
Those already guided receive increased guidance, showing that direction is sustained and augmented after entry onto the way.
The earth is spread so people may traverse its broad roads; it supplies the physical road-field, although no lost traveler or guide is named.
The sun is sworn by together with its morning brightness, ضُحَىٰهَا, naming the light source whose revealing action 91:3 sets against night.
Day is sworn by when it discloses or displays the sun, echoing the source's road that becomes visible in daylight.
Night is sworn by when it covers the sun, reversing 91:3's disclosure and supplying the concealment in which the road disappears.
Quraysh's winter and summer journeys place repeated travel behind the commands about the House, food, and security in the next two ayat.
The travelers are told to worship the Lord of this House, making the home at the center of their journeys the focus of response.
The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and grants safety from fear, placing provision and security at the journey's settled center.

One witness may تَضِلَّ in testimony and be reminded by the other; this may extend the lost-and-guided structure into losing the intended account and being brought back, though no road scene is present.
Jacob sends his sons to search for Joseph and his brother without despairing; it specifically stages people seeking the lost, but it does not say they are unsure which direction to take.
Pharaoh's wife asks God to build her a house near Him in the Garden and save her from Pharaoh; it gives the threatened person a true final home, though no guiding journey is narrated.
When the moon appears and then sets, Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the lost; a night light that fails is set against divine guidance.
The believers' light runs before them and they ask God to perfect it, repeating the image of illumination advancing ahead of travelers toward their promised destination.
Those who hold fast to God are admitted to mercy and guided to Him by a straight path; the light announced in 4:174 becomes a route and destination.
Those who invent comparisons have strayed and cannot find a way, directly joining loss of judgment to inability to locate a route.
Moses' sister walks to those who found him and offers to guide them to a caretaker, so guidance returns the displaced child to his mother and a safe home.
Moses' sister asks whether she should guide Pharaoh's household to a family that will care for the infant; the guide leads those holding the found child toward his true household.
Moses is returned to his mother so that she may be comforted, completing the guided movement from loss back into the home.
God chooses Adam, turns toward him, and guides him immediately before promising in 20:123 that followers of divine guidance will not lose the way.
Those who reject the signs are deaf and dumb in darknesses, while God may place a person on a straight path; failed perception and found direction are set against one another.
A man comes running from the farthest part of the city and tells his people to follow the messengers; he physically arrives to point them toward the guided leaders named in 36:21.
The qiblah objection is answered by saying east and west belong to God and He guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining physical orientation to divine direction.
The sacrificial offering, هَدْيًا, must reach the Kaaba; this different sense of the named ه د ي root still depicts something conducted toward the House as its destination.
The sacrificial offerings, ٱلْهَدْىَ, are prevented from reaching their appointed place; a different sense of the guidance root is bound to a journey blocked short of its destination.
When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, so the night marker sought for road information becomes the place where divine direction is actually encountered.
On reaching the fire Moses hears the blessed call, completing the movement from the distant light of 27:7 to the true source of guidance.
When Moses reaches the fire, he is called from the side of the valley; the hoped-for wayfinding sign becomes an encounter with the divine speaker.
The possible death of the Messenger prompts the question whether his followers will turn back on their heels, making loss of the leader a test of continued direction.
Believers are warned that obeying rejecters will turn them back on their heels and return them as losers; false leadership reverses their course.
The believers flee uphill without turning toward anyone while the Messenger calls them from behind, a battlefield reversal in which followers run away from their guide's call.
When God's signs were recited, the hearers recoiled on their heels; revealed speech that should guide instead triggers the source's backward motion.
One whom God leaves astray has no guide, and such people wander blindly in rebellion; the ayah directly combines absent guide, aimless motion, and impaired sight.
The warned day is described as a day of turning one's backs, when no protector can save and no guide exists for one God leaves astray.
Those left astray have no protector and ask whether there is any road back, making lost guidance inseparable from an unavailable return route.
A seal over hearing and heart and a covering over sight end in the question who can guide after God; obscured perception marks the boundary of finding the way.
The ayah states that one God leaves astray has no guide, isolating the absence of the forward guide as the decisive condition.
No one can lead astray the person God guides, completing 39:36's two-sided boundary between direction and loss.
Those who purchase error in exchange for guidance make a trade that neither profits nor leaves them guided, treating direction as a gift deliberately surrendered.
Turning away from divine remembrance yields a constricted life and resurrection blind, the perceptual and existential reversal of following guidance in 20:123.
Pharaoh's household picks up the river-borne infant, but the ayah names the future enemy and grief within that apparent shelter; being found does not yet mean reaching the right home.
For those whose reckoning is deferred, no refuge will ultimately be found apart from God; delayed arrival does not create another home.
Before the unavoidable day arrives, people are told they will have no refuge and no power to deny their deeds, marking the final boundary on seeking another shelter.
On that day the human being is told there is no place of escape, closing every imagined route away before 75:12 names the true destination.
Night covers Abraham and a star appears, opening the nocturnal search whose failing celestial markers lead to his explicit plea for guidance in 6:77.
The rising sun seems greater but also sets, so even daylight's brightest visible object cannot serve as the ultimate guide sought in the preceding ayah.
Under threat, Lot wishes for power or a strong support to which he could take refuge; the longing for shelter is answered by the messengers' night-route command in 11:81.
God makes night for rest and day sight-giving, giving the source's night and daytime travelers their different fields of visibility.
Night is made for rest and day for seeing, a repeated formulation of the perceptual difference on which the hidden and visible road depends.
Divine mercy appoints night for rest and day for seeking bounty, linking the daylight interval to purposeful movement and provision.
God makes night for rest and day sight-giving, repeating the concrete day-night boundary behind the traveler's ability to choose a road.
Night is made a covering, the concealment that explains why the traveler cannot discern the route before 78:11's active day.
Day is made the time of livelihood, fitting the source's “daytime man” who moves and seeks provision once concealment lifts.
A clear proof and manifest light have come from God; 4:175 identifies the straight route and divine destination disclosed by that light.

Moses describes the staff in his hand as something he leans upon during ordinary use; it is a concrete traveler's staff, though the ayah does not itself call it the forward-going hādiya of the source dictionary.
The command to invite with wisdom and the best manner ends by distinguishing who strays from God's way and who is guided, giving content to guidance as gentle indication.

Moses and Aaron are told to address Pharaoh gently so that he may remember or fear; this is a specific prophetic instance of the source definition of guidance through gentleness, though the ayah does not use هدى.
Abraham asks that the town of the House be secure and its people provided with fruits, extending 2:125's place of return into a safe, provisioned home.
A secure sanctuary is contrasted with people being snatched away around it, presenting the sacred home as refuge at the end of surrounding danger.
God makes the earth an expanse, supplying the traversable ground on which the broad roads of 71:20 run.
God makes Abraham an imam for people after testing him; leadership is not described as road guidance here, but the appointed person stands before a community as the section's guide does.
The Quran guides to what is most upright, letting received speech itself perform the directing role that the guided Prophet later performs for others.
The Book given to Moses is made guidance for the children of Israel, supplying the guidance from which the leaders of 32:24 guide by God's command.
The Book of Moses is described as a leader and mercy, while the confirming Arabic Book warns and gives good news; “leader” gives revelation the forward position of a guide.
The Book of Moses is called a leader and mercy before the Quranic witness, making prior revelation an imam that goes before and directs.
The God who imposed the Quran on the Prophet promises to return him to a place of return, turning the prophetic route into an assured homecoming.
The infant Moses is cast into the river, carried to shore, and taken up under God's watch, staging a displaced child whose route to his true caretaker is completed in 20:40.
Moses' mother is told to place him in the river without fear and is promised that he will be returned, so a dangerous route begins with assurance of homecoming.
Pharaoh's wife asks that the found infant not be killed and imagines adopting him, providing a temporary household before he is guided back to his mother.
Moses' sister is told to follow his trace and watches from afar, a literal act of tracking the lost child that enables the guidance offered in 28:12.
Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful, asking God for rescue; this supplies the displaced traveler whose request for road guidance follows in 28:22.
After reaching Midian and helping the women, Moses withdraws to shade and declares his need for any good God may send, joining arrival with poverty before a home is offered.
At the fire Moses learns that he has reached the sacred valley and is told to remove his sandals, confirming arrival at a destination unlike the practical landmark he expected.
God saves Moses and all who are with him after the sea opens, supplying the successful arrival-side of the divinely guided route.
A brother predicts that a passing caravan will pick Joseph up from the well, anticipating the traveler who finds the displaced boy in 12:19.
Wherever people turn, God's face is there; the ayah addresses orientation when no single visible direction can contain the divine presence.
Whenever the Prophet sets out, he is commanded to turn toward the Sacred Mosque, giving departure a fixed destination and bodily direction.
The sacrificial offering, هَدْى, is not to be interrupted before it reaches its appointed place; this different branch of the named root still carries an object toward a prescribed destination.
Believers may not violate the sacrificial offerings or obstruct visitors heading to the Sacred House for bounty and favor; travelers and the differently sensed هَدْى share the same destination.
Abraham identifies the One who created him as the One who guides him, providing the enduring divine agency behind his later statement that he is going to his Lord.
God chooses Abraham and guides him to a straight path, answering in biographical form the traveler's trust voiced in 37:99.
Children of Adam are told that messengers will recount God's signs and that those who respond need not fear or grieve, repeating the post-descent provision of guidance through human speakers.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best meaning are the ones God has guided, joining received words, following, and guidance.
After every escape is denied in 75:11, this ayah names the final destination as being to the Lord, completing the journey boundary.
